notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Leviticus 8, drawn from the allowed sites.

---

## Leviticus 8 — The Consecration of the Priests

### Overview

This chapter moves from the legal material of Leviticus 1–7 (the sacrifices) into narrative, describing how Moses carried out the commands first given in Exodus 29. The central theme is **consecration to service**, involving purification (washing), preparation (clothing), consecration (anointing), sanctification (blood), dedication ("filling the hands"), and inauguration (the meal). (preceptaustin.org)

---

### v. 1: "Then the LORD said to Moses"

The formula "the LORD spoke to Moses" appears 23 times in Leviticus and signals divine authority for what follows. The literary genre now shifts from legal prescription (chs. 1–7) to historical narrative (chs. 8–10): from "sacred things" to "sacred persons." (preceptaustin.org)

---

### vv. 2–3: The command to assemble the people and bring the items

God tells Moses to take Aaron, his sons, the garments, anointing oil, the bull for the sin offering, two rams, and the basket of unleavened bread—all items already specified in Exodus 29. The "whole congregation" is to be assembled at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. Ellicott notes that "all the congregation" means the elders, heads of tribes, and principal men who represented the people—not literally every Israelite; this is confirmed by Leviticus 9:1, which says Moses called "the elders of Israel." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/8.htm) Guzik notes the ceremony was public because "ministers are to be ordained in the public assembly" (Trapp). The purpose, per Exodus 29:1, was "to hallow them for ministering to Me as priests." (enduringword.com)

---

### vv. 4–5: Moses obeys; the assembly gathers

Moses did exactly as commanded. He announced, "This is what the LORD has commanded to be done"—the whole ceremony was God's plan, not Moses'. Ellicott notes Moses published the instructions given in Exodus 29:1–37 to the assembled people. Tradition recorded that this ceremony took place on the 23rd of the month Adar (February). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/8.htm)

---

### v. 6: The washing of Aaron and his sons

Moses presented Aaron and his sons and washed them with water. Ellicott explains the Hebrew phrase "wash with water" when used without specifying body parts (as in Gen. 19:2, Exod. 30:19–21) denotes bathing the entire body—full immersion. This was done not publicly but in a baptistry behind a curtain. During the Second Temple, priestly immersion required a hollow in the ground containing at least 24 cubic feet of water. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/8.htm)

Guzik calls this a public, humbling act: "We cannot be cleansed from our sin without being humbled first." The washing was a one-time, whole-body cleansing—after this, priests only needed to wash hands and feet. He likens it to the believer's cleansing by God's Word (Eph. 5:26) and the regenerating work of the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5). (enduringword.com)

Spurgeon, preaching from Exodus 29, explains the washing typifies two things: (1) regeneration, "born of water and of the Spirit," making us new creatures; (2) remission of sins by the blood of Christ. He stresses: "He who would serve the Lord must first confess his iniquities and obtain remission, or he can no more approach the living God than a leper could enter into the holy place." (spurgeon.org/sermons/the-consecration-of-the-priests)

Precept Austin cites G. Campbell Morgan: "It is an arresting thing to see him [Moses] thus exercising all the functions of the priestly office, although he was not permanently appointed thereto. The explanation is that he was acting as in the very place of God." (preceptaustin.org)

---

### vv. 7–9: Clothing Aaron in the high-priestly garments

Moses clothed Aaron piece by piece: the tunic, sash, robe, ephod with its woven band, breastpiece with Urim and Thummim, turban, and the gold plate ("Holy to the LORD"). Ellicott notes the linen drawers (Exod. 28:42) are omitted here because Aaron put them on himself behind the curtain after bathing. The ephod was a sleeveless garment of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, worn over the shoulders. The "curious girdle" (band) was woven from the same piece as the ephod itself. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/8.htm)

Guzik emphasizes that the garments were provided by God at no cost to Aaron; similarly, "every believer is clothed in Jesus Christ and in His righteousness," received and worn by faith. Spurgeon says the same: "They were at no expense in buying them, nor labour in weaving them… they had simply to put them on." He adds that these garments were "absolutely necessary"—without them the priest would die (Exod. 28:43), just as a person attempting to serve God without Christ's righteousness "puts himself in a most perilous position." (enduringword.com; spurgeon.org)

---

### vv. 10–13: Anointing the tabernacle and the priests

Moses anointed the tabernacle and everything in it, sprinkling oil on the altar seven times, anointing all utensils and the basin. Poole notes the sevenfold sprinkling signified "the singular use and holiness of it, which it was not only to have in itself, but also to communicate to all the sacrifices laid upon it." (enduringword.com, citing Poole)

Then Moses poured anointing oil on Aaron's head—not sprinkled but poured, signifying the Spirit given in great measure (Ps. 133:2). Ellicott notes this profuse pouring was repeated at every high-priestly succession, while common priests were merely marked with oil on the forehead. During the Second Temple, the anointer drew the Hebrew letter *Kaph* (initial of *Kohen*, "priest") between the eyebrows. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/8.htm)

Precept Austin's William MacDonald note: "The anointing oil was not sprinkled but was 'poured' on Aaron's head, a picture of the Spirit poured without measure upon Jesus, our High Priest." (preceptaustin.org)

Aaron's sons received tunics, sashes, and headbands (v. 13)—simpler garments than the high priest's. Spurgeon notes the common priests' pure white linen was "very comely to look upon," emblematic of "the righteousness of the saints." (spurgeon.org)

---

### vv. 14–17: The sin offering bull

Aaron and his sons laid hands on the bull's head—an act of identification and transfer of sin. Spurgeon notes the Hebrew word implies "pressing hard upon the bullock's head… loading him with their burden, signifying their acceptance of its substitution." (spurgeon.org)

Moses slaughtered it, put blood on the altar's four horns with his finger, purifying the altar, and poured the rest at the base. Ellicott explains that unlike the sin offering for the high priest or congregation (where blood went into the tabernacle—Lev. 4:7, 16–18), here blood was applied only to the altar of burnt offering because Moses was not an Aaronic priest and the newly consecrated priests could not eat their own sin offering. The fat, liver lobe, and kidneys were burned on the altar; the rest—hide, flesh, dung—was burned outside the camp. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/8.htm)

Guzik: "The sin offering said, 'We have failed to give our best to God. This animal now gives its best to atone for our failure.'" The altar (literally "killing-place") was made holy—just as the cross is transformed from a place of death to a place of life. (enduringword.com)

---

### vv. 18–21: The burnt offering ram

Aaron and his sons laid hands on the ram. Moses slaughtered it and sprinkled blood on all sides of the altar. The ram was cut into pieces, the entrails and legs washed, then the entire animal burned. Guzik: "The burnt offering said, 'We have failed to give our all to God. This animal now gives its all to atone for our failure.'" He notes that total commitment could only come after cleansing, anointing, and atonement. (enduringword.com)

Spurgeon contrasts the sin offering (Christ bearing our sin, obnoxious to God, burned outside the camp) with the burnt offering (Christ presenting perfect obedience, a sweet savour, entirely consumed on the altar): "Jesus has rendered to the Father all that he could desire from men, and the Lord is well pleased for his righteousness' sake." A sense of acceptance is necessary for joyful service; without it, "the legal spirit will begin to work to win acceptance by merit, and that will spoil all." (spurgeon.org)

---

### vv. 22–24: The ram of ordination—blood on ear, thumb, and toe

The second ram, "the ram of ordination" (literally "ram of filling"), was brought. Aaron and his sons laid hands on it. Moses slaughtered it and applied blood to Aaron's right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe, then did the same for his sons. The remaining blood was sprinkled on the altar.

Ellicott: the blood on the ear taught the priest "to hearken to the commandments of the Lord"; on the thumb, "to execute God's will"; on the toe, to "walk in the way of His commandments." The right side was chosen as representing what is strongest. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/8.htm)

Guzik: "They should hear differently because the blood was on their ear. They should work differently because the blood was on their thumb. They should walk differently because the blood was on their toe." The right side was considered superior (most people are right-handed), so God wanted their best. (enduringword.com)

Spurgeon: "Moses dipped his finger in the blood, and smeared first the priest's right ear, then his thumb, and then his toe; as Matthew Henry says, as if they marked the boundaries and extremities of man's being, to show that all that was enclosed within the crimson lines was consecrated unto the Lord." The ear was to hear God's commands; the hand to do God's work; the foot to walk in holiness. "The whole man was thus consecrated by the blood of the Everlasting Covenant—a solemn seal, indeed!" (spurgeon.org)

Precept Austin notes that the same parts were touched with blood for the healed leper in Leviticus 14:14–17. (preceptaustin.org)

---

### vv. 25–29: The wave offering

Moses took the fat portions, the fat tail, the right thigh, and from the unleavened bread basket one cake of each kind, placed them on the fat and right thigh, then put all these into the hands of Aaron and his sons and waved them before the LORD. Then Moses took them back and burned them on the altar atop the burnt offering. This was the "ordination offering" (literally "filling offering").

Ellicott explains this is where the term "filling the hands" comes from—the main duty of the priest was to present the worshipper's offering to God; he was inducted into office by the placing of offerings in his hands (cf. Heb. 8:3). (via preceptaustin.org citing Peake)

Moses received the breast as his portion (v. 29) since he officiated as priest. Normally the right thigh belonged to the priests, but in this consecration ceremony it was inappropriate for them to benefit personally. (enduringword.com)

---

### v. 30: Sprinkling of oil and blood on priests and garments

Moses took anointing oil and blood from the altar and sprinkled both on Aaron, his sons, and their garments. This consecrated both persons and vestments.

Spurgeon calls this "that double anointing—the blood of Jesus which cleanses—and the oil of the Holy Spirit which perfumes us. It is well to see how these two blend in one… It is a terrible blunder to set the blood and the oil in opposition, they must always go together." (spurgeon.org)

Ellicott: the garments, as the badge of office, received the same cleansing and sanctification as the priests themselves. He cites Hebrews 9:22: "almost all things were by the law purged with blood." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/8.htm)

---

### vv. 31–32: The fellowship meal

Moses commanded Aaron and his sons to boil the flesh at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting and eat it there with the bread. Any remainder was to be burned.

Guzik: the eating did not begin the consecration—it came after washing, clothing, and blood-atonement. Eating pictures "a healthy, continuing relationship with Jesus": personal (no one can eat for you), inward (you must take it in), active (you cannot eat while asleep), and arising from need, producing satisfaction. (enduringword.com)

Spurgeon likewise: "Let not this distinction be forgotten; the eating of the sacrifice is not intended to give life, for no dead man can eat, but to sustain the life which is there already." (cited at enduringword.com)

Ellicott notes that unlike ordinary peace offerings where the offerer could invite family (Lev. 7:15), here no layman could partake—the flesh and bread were "peculiarly holy" (Exod. 29:33). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/8.htm)

---

### vv. 33–35: Seven days of consecration

Aaron and his sons were not to leave the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for seven full days and nights, until their ordination was complete. The same rites were repeated each day (Exod. 29:36). The warning "so that you will not die" underscored the seriousness of the charge.

Guzik: the seven-day repetition emphasized that even the high priest was a sinner needing atonement. Leaders should be held to a high standard, but not the standard of perfection—pointing to Christ's sinless priesthood. The seven days also typified a complete period of preparation. (enduringword.com)

Ellicott: the command was to stay within the court ("enclosure of the tent of meeting"), not the tabernacle itself. Each day the sin offering, burnt offering, and consecration offering were repeated, along with sprinkling of blood and oil. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/8.htm)

Peake's commentary (via studylight.org) notes that atonement (v. 34) was necessary to "remove all trace of uncleanness, i.e. of whatever was not suitable to such special purposes, previous to the ceremony." The entire intention was "to emphasize the special dedication of both priest and altar, and it may be said to imply the thought of a covenant between Yahweh and the priests." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-8.html)

---

### v. 36: Obedience

"So Aaron and his sons did everything the LORD had commanded through Moses." The chapter ends with simple, complete obedience.

Precept Austin notes this is the conclusion of the narrative, matching the opening emphasis that Moses did all as commanded—the entire ceremony was carried out in exact conformity to God's instructions. (preceptaustin.org)

---

## Distinctive Protestant Tradition Emphases

### Reformed / Baptist (Spurgeon)

Spurgeon's sermon on this chapter stresses the **priesthood of all believers**: "Under the law, only one family could serve God in the priest's office, but under the gospel all the saints are 'a chosen generation, a royal priesthood' (1 Pet. 2:9)." He explicitly rejects any special clergy class: "In the Christian church no persons whatsoever are set apart to the priesthood above the rest of their brethren." The consecration ceremonies therefore typify what happens to every believer: washing (regeneration and forgiveness), clothing (Christ's righteousness), anointing (the Spirit coming through Christ the Head), sin offering (substitutionary atonement), burnt offering (acceptance in Christ), and peace offering (communion with God). (spurgeon.org/sermons/the-consecration-of-the-priests)

### Reformed (Ligonier / R.C. Sproul)

Ligonier recommends Gordon Wenham's commentary as the premier resource on Leviticus. Wenham's central emphasis on Leviticus 8–10 is that "God's greatness and holiness cannot be ignored; he must be acknowledged by our whole being." The theology is that the priesthood mediates between a holy God and sinful people, and every detail of the consecration points to the necessity of holiness in those who draw near. (learn.ligonier.org/articles/the-book-of-leviticus)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)

Guzik emphasizes the **anointing with oil as a picture of the Holy Spirit given in great measure** (poured, not merely sprinkled), and the personal appropriation of these truths by every believer today. The "anointing" (1 John 2:20) belongs to all Christians, and the process of consecration—cleansing, clothing, anointing, sacrifice, and sustained relationship—is directly applied to the believer's spiritual life. The blood on ear, thumb, and toe teaches that consecrated believers should hear, work, and walk differently because they are "stained with the blood of sacrifice." (enduringword.com)

### Anglican (Ellicott)

Ellicott, being an older Anglican scholarly commentary, focuses heavily on the **liturgical and ritual precision**, historical details of Second Temple practice, and careful distinction of Hebrew terms. It treats the chapter as a fulfillment account of Exodus 29 and emphasizes the typological link between the Aaronic priesthood and Christ. Ellicott notes, for instance, that the high priest's anointing with oil poured on the head was repeated at every succession, while common priests were only marked on the forehead—a distinction preserved in Anglican ordination theology regarding bishops versus presbyters. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/8.htm)

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (Peake's Commentary via StudyLight.org)

Peake notes two interesting features: (1) The phrase "fill the hands" (translated "consecrate" or "ordain") is the key term; in Babylonian usage a similar phrase meant "to confer office upon." The action that gives its name to the whole proceeding is not the sprinkling of blood but the placing of offerings into the priests' hands—the priest's primary duty was presenting offerings to Yahweh. (2) The anointing of the tabernacle and altar is not mentioned in Exodus 29, nor is the anointing of Aaron's garments (Lev. 8:30), suggesting these may be later ritual developments added in the Levitical account. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-8.html)

### Catholic and Orthodox Views

I was unable to access the Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) sites within the tool limits for fetching full pages. However, Catholic and Orthodox traditions generally read this chapter as establishing the **sacramental priesthood**, seeing in Aaron and his sons a type of the ordained priesthood of the New Covenant—the bishop (high priest), priests, and deacons. The anointing with oil, the vesting in sacred garments, the laying on of hands, and the seven-day retreat all prefigure elements of Christian ordination rites. The emphasis differs from the Protestant "priesthood of all believers" reading: where Spurgeon sees every believer in these rites, Catholic and Orthodox traditions see the ordained ministerial priesthood specifically.
